lessons.title: उम्र — the same word as Arabic
lessons.gloss: age — the same word as Arabic's ʿumr, borrowed through Persian, beside formal Sanskrit āyu

segments.text: You just met Arabic's ʿumr. Hindi's everyday word for "age" is the exact same word, carried through Persian.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — उम्र — a Perso-Arabic loan, and a native alternative

segments.text: उम्र (umr) = "age" — this is Arabic's ʿumr, borrowed into Hindi through Persian, and it's the everyday, colloquial word most Hindi speakers use. Hindi also has a fully native Sanskrit alternative, आयु (āyu, "age, lifespan"), which feels more formal or literary — a register split you've now seen several times (compare Kannada's Sanskrit-tatsama madhyāhna vs. Tamil's native words for the same concepts, just flipped here: the borrowed word is the everyday one, the native word is the formal one).

segments.instruction: "umr" — age, same word as Arabic's ʿumr
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "umr" — age, same word as Arabic's ʿumr]

segments.text: What language does Hindi's उम्र come from, and what's the native Sanskrit alternative? (Arabic ʿumr, via Persian; native alternative is आयु, āyu.) Which one is ordinary conversational Hindi? (Umr.) Next: use a genitive marker to say how many years someone belongs to.

lessons.title: कितने साल के हो? (kitne sāl ke ho?) — belonging to so many years
lessons.gloss: Hindi tells age as belonging to a number of years, a fifth cross-language shape

segments.text: Languages do not agree on whether age is something you have, are, were born with, or state without a verb. Hindi gives the idea a fifth shape.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — The two sentences

segments.text: तुम कितने साल के हो? — "How old are you?" (informal), literally "you, of how many years, are?" (tum kitne sāl ke ho?)
मैं बीस साल का हूँ। — "I am twenty years old," literally "I [am one] belonging to twenty years." (maiṅ bīs sāl kā hūṅ.)
के/का (ke/kā) is Hindi's genitive postposition, "of, belonging to." The same marker family handles possession elsewhere: merā ghar, "my house."

So Hindi does not copy Romance's "I have years," Germanic's simple "I am [a number]," Latin's "born + N years," or Arabic's verbless "my age [is] N." It says "I am [one] belonging to N years," with a genitive marker plus होना (honā, "to be").

segments.instruction: "tum kitne sāl ke ho?" — how old are you?

segments.instruction: "maiṅ bīs sāl kā hūṅ" — I belong to twenty years
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "maiṅ bīs sāl kā hūṅ" — I belong to twenty years]

segments.text: What does के/का mark? (A genitive/possessive relationship.) Does Hindi use Romance "have," simple Germanic "be," Latin "born," or Arabic's verbless sentence? (None: it says "belonging to N years" + honā.)
